newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean workers seen backing down on pay claim.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean workers seen backing down on pay claim.

text.p: South Korean workers are likely to settle swiftly for a single-digit wage hike this year despite calls by a militant union body for a 10.6 percent rise, economists and financial analysts said on Wednesday.
With the economy slumping, and public sympathy for worker militancy waning, company management will have the upper hand over unions in annual pay talks, they said.
The Korean Confederation of Trade Unions on Tuesday announced it would seek an average 10.6 percent wage rise this year. Wages rose an average 11.9 percent last year.
Leading employers are pushing for a wage freeze in salary negotiations, which usually start in April or May.

"The balance of power is moving in favour of management," said Rhee Namuh, research head at Dongbang Peregrine Securities. "The public will strongly support management this time because it realises firms are hitting rough times.
"If strikes begin, labour unions can expect a massive crackdown by the government with strong public support," Rhee added.
Lee Ju-ho, a labour specialist at the Korea Development Institute, said that in the current economic climate workers would fight harder for job security than pay.
"Employees are likely to settle for a lower rate than last year but will demand job security in return," he said.
South Korean wages have risen by an average of almost 15 percent over the past decade, outpacing productivity gains and eroding corporate competitiveness.
A tough new labour law rammed through parliament last December aimed to restore South Korea's competitive edge by allowing worker layoffs.
However, President Kim Young-sam sent it back to parliament after almost one month of strikes spearheaded by the confederation, and a watered-down version was passed on Monday.
Kim signed the revised bill on Wednesday and it will come into force on Thursday.
"A 10 percent raise demand is totally unacceptable considering current difficulties local companies are facing," said Rhee. Growth of between zero to five percent was appropriate, he said.

Plunging prices of South Korea's major exports, including computer chips, and rising costs of commodity imports have derailed growth. The problems have been exacerbated by a weak yen, which makes rival Japanese exports more competitive.

In the latest gloomy assessment, the Samsung Economic Research Instutute predicted Gross Domestic Product growth this year at 5.0 percent -- the weakest since 1980 -- against an earlier projection of 6.3 percent.
Growth last year was 6.9 percent.

"The business performance of local companies is not likely to get much better this year," said Kim Joo-hyung, an economist at LG Economic Research Institute. "Companies will use this issue to persuade labour unions to compromise.
"Workers are aware of a sense of national economic crisis. This awareness could help companies to settle wage negotiations much faster," Kim said.
This year's strikes cost $3.28 billion in lost production, and leading employers have said they will take this into account in their wage settlements.
The Federation of Korean Industries, which represents the nation's 30 leading business groups, has said it would aim to freeze total wage costs this year at last year's level.
